options.a: Employer-sponsored, pre-tax account for eligible medical expenses; largely use-it-or-lose-it each plan year.
options.b: Individually owned, pre-tax account paired with an HDHP; unused funds roll over and stay with the employee.
options.c: Employer-funded reimbursement account; only the employer contributes and unused balances may carry forward.
options.d: Archer-style medical savings account for self-employed or small-employer workers with a high-deductible plan.

distractorExplanations.b: Describes a health savings account (HSA): HSAs require an HDHP, are owned by the employee, and roll over; an FSA is employer-sponsored and largely use-it-or-lose-it.
distractorExplanations.c: Describes a health reimbursement arrangement (HRA), which only the employer funds; an FSA is funded mainly by employee pre-tax salary reductions.
distractorExplanations.d: Describes an Archer MSA, the older predecessor of the HSA for self-employed and small-employer workers; it is not the employer FSA.

options.a: Coverage for routine cleanings and exams only; fillings, crowns, and oral surgery fall under the medical plan
options.b: Coverage for preventive, basic, and major dental services subject to deductibles, coinsurance, and limits
options.c: Federal health insurance mainly for age 65+, certain disabled persons, and ESRD/ALS eligibility.
options.d: Coverage purchased by individual or family outside employer group, subject to market rules.

distractorExplanations.a: Dental plans cover basic (fillings) and major (crowns) services too, not just preventive care; restorative dentistry is not shifted to the medical plan.
distractorExplanations.c: This is the answer to a different question (“Which of the following best describes Medicare as tested on this exam?”), not to this one.
distractorExplanations.d: This is the answer to a different question (“Which statement correctly describes individual health insurance as tested in health insurance?”), not to this one.

options.a: Preferred provider organization offering network discounts and greater provider flexibility than HMO
options.b: Health condition existing before policy effective date; treatment varies by law and policy type.
options.c: Health maintenance organization emphasizing network care, primary care physician, referrals, and prepaid/capitated structure.
options.d: Exclusive provider organization with no out-of-network coverage except emergencies

distractorExplanations.d: Describes an EPO; a PPO is the plan that still pays (at a higher cost share) when members go out of network.
distractorExplanations.b: This is the answer to a different question (“Which of the following best describes preexisting condition as tested on this exam?”), not to this one.
distractorExplanations.c: Not the best answer here; the right answer is “Preferred provider organization offering network discounts and greater provider flexibility than HMO”.

options.a: Plan with lower premiums and lower deductibles that is paired with an FSA rather than an HSA
options.b: Plan with a high deductible that is paired with an HRA the employee funds through pre-tax salary
options.c: Plan whose high deductible is waived for all services once the member opens an HSA account
options.d: Plan with higher deductible that may be paired with HSA if it meets federal requirements

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the design: an HDHP has a higher deductible (usually with lower premiums) and is the plan type that can be paired with an HSA.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the HSA with an HRA, and HRAs are funded only by the employer, not by employee salary reductions.
distractorExplanations.c: Opening an HSA does not waive the deductible; only preventive care may be covered before the HDHP deductible is met.

options.a: Federal law requiring the group insurer to convert departing employees to individual policies without proof of insurability
options.b: Federal law guaranteeing laid-off workers continued group coverage at the active-employee premium for up to 12 months
options.c: Federal law allowing eligible employees/dependents to continue group health coverage after qualifying events
options.d: Coverage for custodial or skilled care needs due to chronic illness, disability, or cognitive impairment.

distractorExplanations.b: COBRA lets the former employee pay up to 102% of the full group premium, usually for 18-36 months, not the subsidized active rate for 12 months.
distractorExplanations.a: Describes the group conversion privilege (a policy/state-law feature), not COBRA, which continues the same group coverage for a limited period.
distractorExplanations.d: This is the answer to a different question (“Which statement correctly describes long-term care insurance as tested in health insurance?”), not to this one.

options.a: Physician services, outpatient care, preventive services, and durable medical equipment
options.b: Hospital inpatient room and board, skilled nursing, and hospice (the Part A core)
options.c: Outpatient prescription drugs purchased through a private stand-alone drug plan
options.d: Long-term custodial nursing home care for as long as the beneficiary needs it

distractorExplanations.b: Inpatient hospital, skilled nursing, and hospice care are Medicare Part A benefits.
distractorExplanations.c: Stand-alone prescription drug plans are Medicare Part D.
distractorExplanations.d: Medicare does not cover long-term custodial care.

options.a: Total of debts, final expenses, and education costs the family will need
options.b: Present value of future earnings the family would lose
options.c: Cash value the policy is projected to accumulate by the insured's retirement
options.d: The insured's current annual salary multiplied by a fixed factor of ten

distractorExplanations.a: That is the needs approach (DIME-style totals of obligations); human life value measures the insured's lost future earnings.
distractorExplanations.c: Cash value accumulation is a policy feature, not a need estimate; HLV values the economic loss of the insured's future earnings.
distractorExplanations.d: That is a rule-of-thumb income multiple, not HLV, which discounts future earnings (net of personal costs) to present value.

options.a: Whole life is permanent with cash value; term is temporary pure protection
options.b: Whole life pays a death benefit only if the insured dies before age 65
options.c: Term builds cash value faster than whole life because its premiums are lower
options.d: Whole life is sold as group coverage through employers; term is sold to individuals

distractorExplanations.d: Product type does not depend on group vs individual sale; group life is usually term, and whole life is typically individual coverage.
distractorExplanations.c: Level term is pure protection with no cash value; its lower premium is exactly because it builds no savings element.
distractorExplanations.b: Whole life pays whenever death occurs while the policy is in force, typically to age 100 or 121.

options.a: Excludes suicide for the life of the policy, returning only premiums paid
options.b: Limits the death benefit if suicide occurs within the first 5-10 years
options.c: Limits death benefit if suicide occurs within first 1-2 years
options.d: Pays double the face amount if suicide occurs after the contestable period

distractorExplanations.a: The suicide exclusion is temporary (typically 1-2 years); after that period a suicide death is paid in full.
distractorExplanations.b: Uses the wrong period; state law typically caps the suicide exclusion at 1-2 years from issue, mirroring the contestable period.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the suicide clause with an accidental death (double indemnity) rider, which excludes suicide rather than doubling the benefit.

options.a: Life insurance pricing, predicting death rates at each attained age
options.b: Annuity payout pricing, predicting how long annuitants will survive
options.c: Disability and health insurance, predicting sickness and injury rates
options.d: Property loss pricing, predicting fire and windstorm claims by region

distractorExplanations.a: Death rates come from mortality tables; morbidity tables track sickness and injury for health and disability pricing.
distractorExplanations.b: Annuity pricing relies on longevity/mortality tables (how long people live), not on morbidity (sickness and disability) rates.
distractorExplanations.d: Fire and windstorm frequency is property-casualty loss data; morbidity is the rate of illness and injury among insureds.

options.a: Driving record, territory, vehicle type, and usage
options.b: Health history, height, weight, and tobacco use
options.c: Race, religion, and national origin of the driver
options.d: Vehicle purchase price alone, ignoring driver history

distractorExplanations.b: These are life and health underwriting factors; auto classification rests on driving record, territory, vehicle, and usage.
distractorExplanations.c: These are prohibited rating factors under state unfair discrimination laws and cannot be used to classify auto risks.
distractorExplanations.d: Vehicle value affects physical damage premium, but driver record, territory, and usage are core classification factors too.

options.a: The share of each premium the agent keeps as commission
options.b: The maximum loss the insurer keeps before reinsurance applies
options.c: The percentage of claims the insurer pays within 30 days
options.d: The minimum capital a state requires the insurer to hold

distractorExplanations.a: Agent commission is unrelated to how much risk the insurer retains.
distractorExplanations.c: Claim payment speed is a service measure, not a retention limit.
distractorExplanations.d: Minimum capital is a solvency requirement, not a retention limit.

options.a: Speculative risk involves chance of gain, loss, or no change and is generally not insurable
options.b: Speculative risk involves chance of gain or loss and is insurable when losses are predictable
options.c: Speculative risk involves only chance of loss or no loss and is the type insurers cover
options.d: Speculative risk is a condition that increases the likelihood or severity of a loss

distractorExplanations.b: Predictability does not make speculative risk insurable; because it carries a chance of gain, insurers cover pure risk instead.
distractorExplanations.c: That definition describes pure risk, the insurable kind; speculative risk adds the possibility of gain.
distractorExplanations.d: That is the definition of a hazard (physical, moral, or morale), not of speculative risk.

options.a: The values exchanged are unequal—a small premium may yield a large benefit or none if no loss occurs
options.b: Only the insured makes a legally enforceable promise, while the insurer's promises are optional
options.c: The insurer drafts the policy on a take-it-or-leave-it basis, so ambiguities favor the insured
options.d: Each party must disclose material facts honestly because both rely on the other's statements

distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the unilateral feature: only the insurer makes an enforceable promise; and unilateral is a different trait from aleatory.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes a contract of adhesion, a separate characteristic; aleatory refers to the unequal exchange of values.
distractorExplanations.d: That is utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei); aleatory means the premium and potential benefit are unequal and contingent.

options.a: A financial or emotional interest in the continued life/health of insured or avoidance of loss, required at policy inception for life insurance.
options.b: Authority to act for insurer can be express, implied, or apparent, subject to law and appointment.
options.c: Insurance relies on each party giving equal value, so premiums must match the expected claim amount
options.d: Insurance relies on truthful disclosure by applicant and insurer because each depends on information from the other

distractorExplanations.c: Describes a commutative exchange; insurance is aleatory (unequal values), and utmost good faith concerns honest disclosure.
distractorExplanations.a: Not the best answer here; the right answer is “Insurance relies on truthful disclosure by applicant and insurer because each depends on information from the other”.
distractorExplanations.b: Not the best answer here; the right answer is “Insurance relies on truthful disclosure by applicant and insurer because each depends on information from the other”.

options.a: The first of the two insureds dies, leaving the survivor
options.b: Either insured becomes disabled and cannot pay premiums
options.c: The second of the two insureds dies; often used for estate taxes
options.d: The policy's cash value reaches the face amount at maturity

distractorExplanations.a: Paying at the first death describes a first-to-die (joint life) policy.
distractorExplanations.b: Disability of an insured does not trigger a life insurance death benefit.
distractorExplanations.d: Cash value reaching face amount is policy endowment, not a survivorship death benefit.

options.a: Annuity where income payments begin at future date after accumulation period.
options.b: Payments continue over lives of two annuitants, often reducing after first death depending on option
options.c: Payments continue for one annuitant's life and stop at death, with no refund to any beneficiary
options.d: Payments continue for a set 10 or 20 years to the annuitant or a beneficiary, then stop

distractorExplanations.c: That is the straight life (life only) option; joint and survivor covers two lives and continues after the first death.
distractorExplanations.d: Describes a period certain option, which guarantees a number of years rather than income over two annuitants' lives.
distractorExplanations.a: Not the best answer here; the right answer is “Payments continue over lives of two annuitants, often reducing after first death depending on option”.

options.a: Adhesion where only insurer has duties
options.b: Equal exchange of values between the parties
options.c: Indemnity limiting life benefits to proven loss
options.d: Utmost good faith requiring full disclosure

distractorExplanations.c: Life insurance is a valued contract paying the face amount; indemnity (paying only the actual loss) applies to property and medical expense coverage.
distractorExplanations.b: Describes a commutative contract; insurance is aleatory, and the doctrine requiring full disclosure is utmost good faith.

options.a: Coverage may begin on the receipt date if the applicant is later found insurable as applied
options.b: Coverage begins only on policy delivery, once the first premium has been paid in full
options.c: Coverage starts on the receipt date even if the applicant is later declined by underwriting
options.d: Coverage is bound for a set period during underwriting even if the applicant proves uninsurable

distractorExplanations.b: That is the result with no receipt at all; a conditional receipt can start coverage earlier, on the application or exam date.
distractorExplanations.c: A conditional receipt gives coverage only if the applicant is found insurable as applied; a declined applicant has no coverage.
distractorExplanations.d: Describes a binding (temporary) receipt, a different receipt type that covers for a period whether or not the applicant qualifies.

options.a: Only a signed client statement that the old policy has already lapsed
options.b: Written approval from the existing insurer before the new policy issues
options.c: Disclosure forms comparing existing and proposed coverage, per state rules
options.d: The agent to wait until the old policy lapses before taking an application

distractorExplanations.a: Replacement rules require a notice/comparison form and notice to the existing insurer, not just a statement about the old policy.
distractorExplanations.b: The existing insurer is notified, but its approval is not required.
distractorExplanations.d: Letting the old policy lapse first could leave the client uninsured; rules require disclosure, not a lapse.

options.a: At issue for life insurance; at the time of loss for property
options.b: At claim payment only, for every line of insurance
options.c: At policy surrender or maturity, for life insurance
options.d: At the insured's death for life insurance; at policy issue for property

distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the rule: life requires insurable interest at issue (not at death), while property requires it at the time of loss.
distractorExplanations.b: Timing differs by line: life at issue, property at the time of loss.
distractorExplanations.c: Life insurable interest is required at issue, not at surrender or maturity.

options.a: Select a primary care physician and obtain referrals for most specialist care
options.b: Use any provider in or out of network at the same cost without referrals
options.c: Submit claim forms for each visit and wait for fee-for-service reimbursement
options.d: Obtain a referral from the insurer before receiving any emergency room care

distractorExplanations.b: That describes an indemnity-style or open plan; HMOs restrict benefits to network providers and use PCP referrals.
distractorExplanations.c: Claim forms and fee-for-service reimbursement belong to traditional indemnity plans; HMOs pay network providers directly or by capitation.
distractorExplanations.d: Emergency care does not require a referral under HMO rules; referrals apply to nonemergency specialist visits.

options.a: Free lifetime health coverage after any voluntary or involuntary job loss
options.b: Former employees to switch into Medicare in place of employer group coverage
options.c: Unlimited continuation of group coverage at the employee's old premium
options.d: Former employees to keep group health coverage temporarily at their own cost

distractorExplanations.b: Job loss does not trigger Medicare eligibility; COBRA continues the employer group plan itself for a limited period.
distractorExplanations.a: COBRA is temporary and the former employee pays the premium.
distractorExplanations.c: COBRA is time-limited (typically 18–36 months) and the person pays up to 102% of the full premium.

options.a: Federal health insurance program for people age 65 and over
options.b: Private Medicare supplement coverage sold by licensed agents
options.c: State workers' compensation benefit for job-related injuries and illness
options.d: Joint federal-state program for low-income eligible individuals

distractorExplanations.a: That describes Medicare; Medicaid is the joint federal-state program based on financial need, not age alone.
distractorExplanations.b: That describes Medigap; Medicaid is a government program administered by the states, not a privately sold product.
distractorExplanations.c: Workers' compensation covers occupational injury; Medicaid is need-based health coverage funded jointly by federal and state government.
